(1) animal models of Alzheimer's do not have predictive validity; (2) animal experiments can be important for the understanding of the disease; and (3) animal experimentation is not a prerequisite for drug development.
animal experimentation contributes to our understanding of Alzheimer's disease, but that it is not a good predictor for drug development.
animal models are not useful for the discovery and development of drugs for AD.

the development of a quantitative (sub) model of the disease, the development of a clinical trial suited for the evaluation of the mechanism of action, and the integration of both in a clinical trial.
the development of a mathematical model of Alzheimer's disease, which will allow us to test hypotheses about the disease and its treatment, to design clinical trials, and to analyze the results.
the development of quantitative models that are able to predict the effect of a drug in a specific disease state.

the animal models of Alzheimer's are not useful in the development of drug treatments for Alzheimer's disease.
the animal model of Alzheimer's disease is a model for a disease that is not known.
the use of animal disease models in drug development for Alzheimer's disease has been disappointing.

the current animal models of Alzheimer's do not contribute to drug development.
the current animal models have been useful in generating hypotheses and in identifying targets, but have not been useful in the development of efficacious treatments.

animal models of Alzheimer's have been used in the wrong way, and that their role should be redefined.
